US housing affordability is deteriorating:

The average 30Y fixed mortgage rate rose +3 basis points last week, to 6.69%, the highest since July 2025.

The 30Y fixed mortgage rate could rise to 7% for the first time since January 2025 before year-end if current inflationary pressures persist.

The US housing affordability crisis is worsening.

Big Tech's AI spending is rising to levels rarely seen in modern history:

Amazon, $AMZN, Alphabet, $GOOGL, Meta, $META, Microsoft, $MSFT, and Oracle, $ORCL, are estimated to increase CapEx by +1.0 percentage point of US GDP in 2026, to a record 2.4%.

To put this into perspective, Big Tech CapEx stood at 0.8% of GDP in 2024, the same level telecom CapEx recorded in 1997.

The AI investment boom is materially exceeding the capital spending surge of the Dot-Com era.

The audit will begin shortly after Aug. 20 and take "several months," delaying Batch Zero classification and the planned September study start. But ERCOT is taking steps to preserve Q1/Q2 2027 energization dates for the most advanced projects -->

>ERCOT is keeping the April 9, 2027 Batch Zero study deadline for now.»

>ERCOT had planned to finalize its long-term load forecast using Batch Zero Base Load by mid-August. It will now wait for the audit and verified Base Load classifications rather than switch to an alternative forecasting method. ERCOT says this will produce a "more accurate and realistic" forecast.

My read: ERCOT is working to preserve the existing timeline for the most advanced projects.

($HUT's 1GW Beacon Point is worth watching here. It targets Q1 2027 initial energization, has an executed AEP Texas interconnection agreement, and has been expected to qualify as Base Load. The campus has up to $50.2B of contracted lease value including extensions, with NVIDIA reportedly the tenant.

ERCOT doesn't identify the six Q1 projects, so we can't confirm Beacon Point is among them. But it fits the profile.)

Show me the NINJA loan.

The defining feature of the subprime bubble was credit extended without verified income to service it: No-income/no-doc mortgages were then pooled, securitized, tranched and spread throughout the global financial system.

The closest data-center equivalent would be a loan against unleased powered land, with no tenant, no rent and no income.

Find me one of those that's been securitized.

Take $KEEL, which reported today. It is advancing three priority sites before leases using balance-sheet capital and ~$1B of unsecured corporate converts. The debt sits at the corporate level, isn't secured by the unleased projects, and comes with an equity conversion feature. Keel says explicitly that lease execution enables the transition to project-level financing backed by long-term contracted cash flows.

$CIFR and $WULF show the same sequencing: CIFR signed Fluidstack/Google at Barber Lake, THEN raised $1.7B of secured project bonds. WULF signed Fluidstack/Google at Lake Mariner, THEN raised $3.2B of secured debt.

Those are direct project bonds sold to institutional investors, not pools of unleased data-center loans sliced into AAA/mezzanine tranches.

Actual data-center securitizations exist too. QTS issues tranched ABS. But those securities are backed by real estate and tenant lease payments. There is income underneath them.

Income first. Project leverage second.

That's not to say these investments are riskless. Hardly! Powered-shell equity is among the riskiest stuff in the public markets today. Power can get delayed, tenants can disappear, construction costs can blow out and $/MW valuations can collapse.

But so far, the no-income development risk is largely sitting where you'd expect it: with equity holders and corporate risk capital. 

Once the industry starts making large asset-level loans against unleased powered land, pooling them, tranching them and distributing them throughout the financial system, I'll take the 2007 analogy much more seriously.

Until then: show me the NINJA loan.
